name: Sugar
description: Plain sugar (sucrose) is not directly poisonous to cats, but it offers no nutritional value and can lead to significant long-term health issues. Cats lack the taste receptors to taste sweetness, so they are not naturally drawn to sugary foods. Regular consumption can contribute to obesity, dental problems, and diabetes. The more immediate danger comes from sugar substitutes, particularly xylitol. This artificial sweetener is commonly found in sugar-free products like gum, candy, peanut butter, and baked goods. While xylitol is famously toxic to dogs, causing a rapid insulin release and life-threateningly low blood sugar, cats do not appear to be affected the same way: veterinary sources report that cats are not at risk of xylitol-induced hypoglycemia or liver injury, and experimental doses up to 1,000 mg/kg produced no toxic effects beyond transient drooling. As a sensible precaution, it is still best to keep xylitol products away from cats. While a tiny, accidental taste of plain sugar is not a cause for panic, it's a good practice to keep all sweets away from cats. Always check the labels on 'sugar-free' or 'diet' human foods for xylitol. If you suspect your cat has ingested any product containing xylitol, contact your veterinarian for guidance.
safetyNotes: Not toxic in small amounts: cats cannot taste sweetness and rarely seek out sugar voluntarily
Metabolic risk: regular sugar intake causes blood sugar dysregulation, obesity, and diabetes in cats
Dental risk: sugar promotes dental plaque and periodontal disease

Xylitol note: sugar-free products use xylitol instead of sugar — xylitol is severely toxic to dogs, but cats are not at risk of xylitol-induced hypoglycemia or liver injury; keep it away as a precaution and check labels
A tiny accidental taste of plain sugar is not an emergency; keep sugary foods away as a general practice

symptoms.name: Regular refined sugar is not acutely poisonous to cats, but it is an inappropriate food that causes long-term health issues. However
Mild Gastrointestinal Upset (From Artificial Sweeteners)
symptoms.notes: While artificial sweeteners like stevia, maltitol, sorbitol, sucralose, and saccharin are not chemically dangerous or poisonous to cats, consuming them in very high amounts can trigger mild gastrointestinal distress and tummy upsets.

symptoms.name: Transient Salivation (From Xylitol Exposure)
symptoms.notes: In dogs, xylitol causes a massive release of insulin leading to fatal hypoglycemia and liver failure.

symptoms.name: Hypoglycemia and Liver Damage (Theoretical/Precautionary for Xylitol)
symptoms.onset: Not documented in cats (the 15-30 minute hypoglycemia / up to 12 hour liver-injury window is the canine profile; cats are not at risk per veterinary sources).
symptoms.notes: Although clinical studies have demonstrated that cats are naturally resistant to xylitol toxicity1., some veterinary sources warn that it is not impossible for an individual cat to be unusually susceptible to the toxin.

symptoms.name: Chronic Metabolic Issues (From Regular Sugar)
symptoms.onset: Chronic (develops progressively over months or years).
symptoms.notes: Regular sugar (sucrose) does not cause acute poisoning symptoms. However, if a cat is regularly fed sugary foods or candies, it will lead to unhealthy weight gain, tooth decay, and the eventual development of feline diabetes.
